description.narrative:
Insatsen ska utveckla och stärka ett integrerat system för social trygghet med fokus på utsatta barn i Etiopien. Förmedling av kontantstöd ska bidra till ökad inkomst för utsatta grupper, samtidigt som uppbyggnad av en system-ansats för social trygghet kommer att bidra till att stärka de långsiktiga effekterna för fattigdomsminskning.
Insatsen ska leda till att fler barn omfattas av social trygghet och till ökad prioritering av offentlig social trygghet riktad till barn. Den förväntas också leda till mer effektiv koordinering inom systemet för social trygghet på nationell och regional nivå, samt till att skapa och sprida kunskap om effekter av social trygghet. Insatsen ska dessutom utveckla rurala och urbana program för social trygghet så att de förmår expandera sin räckvidd och sitt stöd vid Etiopiens återkommande akuta kriser som leder till ökad sårbarhet hos utsatta grupper.
Utvecklingen av ett effektivt system för social trygghet bedöms som en nyckelfråga för att uppnå långsiktigt hållbar minskning av barnfattigdom. När mottagare och deras barn länkas till grundläggande samhällsservice (som utbildning och hälsa) utifrån sina behov kommer det att leda till en generell förbättring av livskvalitet och välmående för de mest utsatta grupperna i samhället.
Regeringens kapacitet kommer att stärkas för att koordinera ett integrerat system för social trygghet och för att etablera och hantera ett informationssystem som länkar mottagare med skräddarsydd service och genom utbildning av socialarbetare som kan bidra till att identifierade mottagare får tillgång till service och möjligen också kan stärka sin egen inkomstgenerering.

The intended outcomes for the intervention is to strenghten a comprehensive integrated and child-sensitive social protection system in Ethiopia. The project is expected to lead to an increased number of children covered by social protection and increased public social protection expenditure for children. While cash transfers will lead to an increased income for identified beneficiaries, the system approach will support a long-term impact for poverty reduction.
The development of an effective social protection system is assessed as key to achieve sustainable reduction of child poverty. When beneficiaries and their children are linked to essential basic services according to their specific needs, this will lead to a general improvement of the lives of the most vulnerable who will be able to access basic services and targeted support.
The government and supply-side will also benefit from the systems approach through development of a standardised MIS, Management Information System, that can systematically link identified beneficiaries of the programme to tailor-made services and through development of a solid social workforce that can ensure that identified beneficiaries can access adequate services and possibly also build sustainable livelihoods.
Strengthening of a shock-responsive system of social protection that can respond early to emerging crises and increased vulnerability will contribute to strengthen resilience of people living in poverty. The development of a more shock-responsive social protection system is also expected to reduce the need for short-term humanitarian support.

The identified overall objectives for the project are: - SDG 1.3: Implement nationally appropriate social protection systems and measures for all, including floors, and by 2030 achieve substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable - UNDAP (2016-2020) By 2020 the Government of Ethiopia uses a social protection systems approach which ensures increased access to a comprehensive package of social protection programmes, interventions and services to poor and vulnerable citizens coping with social and economic risks, vulnerabilities and deprivations. - UNICEF CP (2016-2020) By 2020, Government capacity to develop, implement, coordinate and monitor a national. child-sensitive social protection system strengthened. Additional result ------------------------------- 1. To ensure effective and efficient implementation and management of child-sensitive social protection system within the of the ISNP and the overall sector in rural and urban areas through an increased focus on linkages creation to complementary social services as well as the integration of health care financing into the national social protection agenda as well as the core ISNP components. 2. To ensure maximum and multifaceted impact of the ISNP in rural and urban areas through the expansion of core ISNP programme components to one additional rural woreda in Amhara Region and one additional city. 3. To improve the effectiveness of PSNP’s response to shocks for both PSNP and non-PSNP households with children affected by malnutrition through contributing to the Federal Contingency Budget as well as advocacy at federal level. Expected results; i. Establishment of a comprehensive Linkages and Referral System as part of the urban (UPSNP) and rural (PSNP) Safety Net Programmes with a focus on direct support and destitute groups ii. Integration of health care financing (Community-based Health Insurance - CBHI) into the National Social Protection Agenda through successful piloting of harmonized implementation of the PSNP/UPSNP and the CBHI iii. Establishment of effective and efficient coordination and management of child-sensitive safety nets system at federal and regional level iv. Establishment of Social Workforce (social workers) System and CSO/NGO Collaboration v. Successful ISNP implementation in three rural woredas of Amhara. vi. Successful ISNP implementation in two urban centres of Ethiopia including Addis Ababa vii. Effective use of Federal PSNP Contingency Budget for households in PSNP woredas with malnourished children.

Examples of results
Awaiting the agreed certified financial statement a draft completion memo is already drafted in Trac. The text below, summarising results from the program, will also be available in the Completion Memo.
From 2017 to 2024 ISNP has contributed to integrated policy and programming in the social protection sector. The total contribution from Sida was SEK 406,200,000. The programme launched pilots in rural and urban areas, developed tools and guidelines and built systems for linkage to essential social services under the governmental urban and rural safety net programmes, including health, education, and nutrition. It also made significant progress in developing the capacities of the social service workforce to support case management and referrals in communities.
Over the course of programme implementation, Ethiopia has faced a series of overlapping crises, including conflict, drought, the COVID-19 pandemic, and macroeconomic challenges such as inflation. In order to adapt the Swedish portfolio and meet the needs in new target groups Sida has decided to add funding and new target groups to the program almost every year. This made ISNP relevant through all recent crisis in Ethiopia and Sida has in strategy reports referred to the program to be the flagship of the Swedish portfolio. UNICEFs adaptability and agility were critical in addressing the emerging vulnerabilities from these multiple overlapping shocks, including providing humanitarian assistance in some of the most remote areas and to the hardest-to-reach.
There are very many examples of results. Related to programme design and delivery the ISNP programme has for example:
- strengthened policy coherence and future direction when providing technical support for the gap analysis of the National Social Protection Policy (NSPP) and multi-stakeholder consultations and policy dialogue in 2024. Key recommendations include adopting a life-cycle and rights-based approach, enhancing responsiveness to shocks, improving inter-agency coordination, and expanding coverage to informal workers.
- enhanced integrated social protection in PSNP-5 and PSNP-6. The PSNP is led by the Ministry of Agriculture while the MoWSA is responsible for social protection. Only in PSNP-5 MoWSA was formally integrated in the implementation structure.
- served as a model for integrating cash transfers with access to health, nutrition, and protection services. Drawing from evidence in ISNP pilot sites in Addis Ababa and Amhara core elements particularly the role of social workers were embedded into the design of PSNP-5.
- designed and rolled out of updated gender social development nutrition materials tailored for the PSNP context such as the development and endorsement of new guidance on gender based violence (GBV) case management, Gender, Social Development, and Nutrition (GSD-N) and Social Behaviour Change (SBC) packages.
- elevated MoWSAs role in the implementation of the Urban Productive Safety Net and Job Programme (UPSNJP) for example today MoWSA is the formally designated lead implementer for the Permanent Direct Support (PDS) and the Urban Destitute components of the UPSNJP.
- successfully scaled up the Community-Based Health Insurance (CBHI). Today the total enrolment exceeds 11 million households (approximately 55.7 million individuals, of whom 48 per cent or estimated 27.7 million children), with 2.57 million classified as indigent households, benefiting from fee waivers.
In relation to systems strengthening ISNP has:
- established and operationalised a Federal Social Protection Platform (FSPP) chaired by the MoWSA. The platform, established in 2020, is since serving as a coordination body bringing together government stakeholders, development partners, and civil society.
- strengthened the institutional capacity of MoWSA for example in support of the development of training materials on coordination, grievance mechanisms, reporting, and communications. Support also included legislative frameworks, resource mapping, M&E systems, and partnership strategies.
- strengthened capacity of federal and sub-national structures for effective delivery of design, delivery and monitoring of shock-responsive social protection.
- strengthened the social service workforce for example through training on topics on social protection and linkage to essential social services including social policy, targeting, grievance redress mechanisms (GRM), gender-responsive programming, identification of disability, linkage of cash transfer (including PSNP) beneficiaries to CBHI, health and nutrition services, education, case management, GBV referrals, harmful traditional practices (e.g., child marriage), financial inclusion and Self-Help Groups (SHGs).
The ISNP has developed innovative approaches such as:
- agile and adaptive social protection that could ensure vertical and horizontal expansion during COVID-19. For example in 2020 cash top-ups were provided to 50,050 PDS beneficiaries across 11 cities for a period of six months. Lessons learned from the COVID crisis was used after the next crisis and when integrating IDPs into the program. In 2021, the UPSNJP accommodated coverage of IDPs in the programme and in 2023, the programme covered 770,397 IDPs through unconditional temporary cash transfers. Beside innovations in targeting a digital monitoring system was introduced. Such innovations were developed in cooperation with the Government structures and partners to enhance local ownership and sustainability.
- the development of digital and data driven systems. The following have been achieved between 2017 and 2024: 1) Development of the Integrated Social Affairs Management Information System (IASMIS) with the MoWSA: IASMIS is a web-based application that covers data from five subsystems: urban destitute, elderly, family, persons with disabilities and IDPs. 2) Development of the social service workforce (SSW) dashboard and database: A national SSW monitoring system was developed to display figures and information on workforce distribution, population coverage by the SSW, and capacity gaps. 3) Integration of National ID registration in the implementation of Shock Responsive Cash Transfers (SRCTs): As part of beneficiary verification, the National ID registration was integrated into the SRCT delivery process.
- recognizing the need to augment shock response with early recovery, financial inclusion and economic empowerment and preventive resilience in the social protection system, ISNP piloted the Cash-Plus Financial Inclusion intervention in Oromia Region in 2023 to link humanitarian cash assistance with access to finance and livelihood support.
- recognising the need to enhance gender integration in 2024, ISNP piloted a gender-transformative feature as part of the Cash Plus intervention titled Male engagement sessions. More than 500 boys and men in Amhara Region, including SRCT beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries, were grouped into 27 age-specific groups and attended numerous guided community conversations on positive masculinity, reproductive health, time use, traditional gender roles, GBV and various social norms.
Finally the ISNP has leveraged partnerships:
- with civil society organizations. To reach the most vulnerable populations and expand service delivery, ISNP leveraged strategic partnerships with civil society organizations (CSOs) including with 1) JeCCDO to support integration of Early Childhood Development (ECD), gender and social development into safety net programmes; establishment and capacity-building of self-help groups (SHGs) to support income-generating activities (IGAs); and coordination and delivery of services for the Urban Destitute component of UPSNJP; and 2) Hope for Justice to strengthen implementation of the Urban Destitute component of UPSNJP.
- in 2023 and 2024, the ISNP prioritized economic empowerment as a resilience strategy for vulnerable households. Through partnership with Cooperative Bank of Oromia (COOP), ISNP piloted a Cash-Plus Financial Inclusion intervention, combining shock-responsive cash transfers (SRCTs) with financial literacy, life skills, goal-setting and access to uncollateralised loans. In 2024, this intervention was modified slightly by providing capital funds to SHGs to enable SRCT members to build savings, access credit, and invest in individual and collective income generating activities. The partnership with COOP is now extended to six financial service providers (FSPs).
